newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-De Silguy says EMU delay legally impossible.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-De Silguy says EMU delay legally impossible.

text.p: European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Thursday that any delay to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would be legally impossible and would require a change to the Maastricht treaty.

In a speech to French farmers in Toulouse, southern France, he also said that the move towards launching a single currency in January 1999 was now irreversible and no politician was seriously considering a delay.

"Delay would be legally impossible -- the treaty states clearly that 'the third phase begins on January 1, 1999'. To change the date, you have to change the treaty," de Silguy, who is responsible for economic and monetary affairs, said.

Economic convergence between countries in Europe was progressing, helped by an acceleration in growth, and budget deficits were being reduced, he said. Administrations, banks and companies were stepping up their technical preparations.
"The process leading to Economic and Monetary Union is therefore irreversible today. A significant number of member states will be ready at the appropriate time.

"All speculation about an eventual delay to the timetable which one hears frequently at the moment, notably in France, is both useless and unneccessary. There is moreover not one single politician who is considering it seriously," he said.

Speculation about a delay to EMU has been fuelled by doubts about whether Germany, meant to be Europe's model economy, can cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year to meet Maastricht treaty criteria.

German officials themselves have stoked that speculation by saying, in the words of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, that "convergence determines the timetable" -- suggesting that strict fulfilment of Maastricht criteria could take precedence over the January 1, 1999 launch date.
That in turn has led to a tough legal debate about whether delay to EMU would require an amendment to the treaty.
French officials believe it would, implying renegotiation of the treaty, new referenda and parliamentary debates -- all of which could put EMU off for many, many years.

At issue is a clause in the treaty which states that "if by the end of 1997 the date for the beginning of the third stage (EMU launch) has not been set, the third stage shall start on January 1, 1999."
Some have interpreted this to mean that if another start date beyond 1999 is agreed before the end of this year, EMU could be delayed without amending the Maastricht treaty.
But most senior officials, including the European Commission's own legal experts, argue this is not a proper reading of the treaty.

Others have also argued that even if European Union leaders decided to ignore the legal constraints, they would probably have to agree unanimously to overturn them -- unlikely when so many countries are committed to EMU.
De Silguy said delay would be politically dangerous. "It would open the way to a major European crisis. For it would show that the European Union is not capable of respecting its commitments."
It would also be "economically suicidal", encouraging intense pressure to ease up on budgetary restraint.
"Delay would lead unavoidably to a rise in interest rates, a worsening in unemployment, and undoubtedly monetary turbulence..." he added.
